verdicts.reason: Descriptive definition of alerts; nothing testable on an interface.
Quote says 'should instantiate'; it is a design/integration guideline, not a slave behaviour checkable in simulation.
Optional clocking scheme; scenario covers both.
Sender drives alert_p/n and receiver drives ack; the full handshake with repeats is a multi-cycle protocol, best exercised as a scenario; it is not a single-cycle assertion from one actor.
Stated guarantee: no alert lost across async boundary with any clock ratio; scenario with varied clock ratios.
Sender repeats the alert message while the event stays true; checkable both ways.
Quote states 'will wait for 2 cycles' (a fixed interval); checkable by assertion on the interface but also needs a scenario to drive repeated alerts. Ambiguous which two cycles are counted.
Directly stated: alert immediately propagated to alert_o after the initial level change is synchronized, even under manipulated handshake.
Both modes permitted; scenario exercises both.
Quote says synchronizer flops 'may be omitted'; the protocol staying the same is the requirement, so this is not a hard MUST on omission. Protocol equivalence is the testable part.
Receiver asserts integ_fail_o on incorrectly encoded alert_tx_i.alert_p/n.
Sender signals bad ping/ack encoding via alert_p/n set to same value, toggling continuously, triggering integ_fail_o.
Stated guarantee that lock-up leads to integrity alert or eventually pingfail alert; scenario with fault injection.

duplicates.reason: Both state that the sender/receiver may be used synchronously or asynchronously; they differ only in wording (the 1.3.1 quote adds a rationale).

questions.question: How are the 2 wait cycles between handshakes counted, and does it depend on the clock mode (sync vs async)?
How long may a protocol lock-up persist before the pingfail alert must fire, i.e. what is the bound on 'eventually'?
When a sender-side encoding error is signalled by alert_p/n being set to the same value and toggling, is the toggling period specified?
